claims.claim: The PD microbiome shows decreased abundance of health-promoting bacteria and an increase in pro-inflammatory pathogenic bacteria.
claims.source: Additionally, several studies have detected differences in gut microbiome composition between PD patients and healthy controls (Çamcı and Oğuz, 2016; Keshavarzian et al., 2015; Scheperjans et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2014), with decreased abundance of health-promoting bacteria and an increase in pro-inflammatory pathogenic bacteria in the PD microbiome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on PD microbiome composition.

claims.claim: Altering the microbiome in α-synuclein overexpressing (ASO) mice modulates brain pathology and motor performance.
claims.source: Altering the microbiome in α-synuclein overexpressing (ASO) mice modulates brain pathology and motor performance (Sampson et al., 2016), and gut bacterial species have been shown to accelerate disease in other PD mouse models (Choi et al., 2018; Sampson et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sampson et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Gut bacterial species have been shown to accelerate disease in PD mouse models.
claims.source: Altering the microbiome in α-synuclein overexpressing (ASO) mice modulates brain pathology and motor performance (Sampson et al., 2016), and gut bacterial species have been shown to accelerate disease in other PD mouse models (Choi et al., 2018; Sampson et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2018 and Sampson et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Antibiotic treatment improves motor symptoms in several models of PD.
claims.source: Additionally, antibiotic treatment improves motor symptoms in several models of PD (Cui et al., 2022; Pu et al., 2019; Sampson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2022; Pu et al., 2019; and Sampson et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Microglia can shape neural circuity through regulation of neurogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination.
claims.source: One potential target of gut-brain signaling in PD are microglia, a versatile macrophage-like population of brain cells that can shape neural circuity through regulation of neurogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination (Anderson and Vetter, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson and Vetter, 2019.

claims.claim: In PD and other neurodegenerative conditions, microglial cellular repair responses become dysregulated, resulting in heightened reactivity and chronic inflammation that drives neurodegeneration.
claims.source: In PD and other neurodegenerative conditions, microglial cellular repair responses are thought to become dysregulated, ultimately resulting in heightened reactivity and chronic inflammation that drives neurodegeneration (Troncoso-Escudero et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Troncoso-Escudero et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Microglia respond to signals from the periphery including from the gut microbiome.
claims.source: Microglia respond to signals from within the brain, but also receive input from the periphery including from the gut microbiome (Abdel-Haq et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abdel-Haq et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Offspring of germ-free (GF) mice show differences in microglial gene expression and chromatin accessibility compared to specific-pathogen-free (SPF) counterparts.
claims.source: Offspring of germ-free (GF) mice show differences in microglial gene expression and chromatin accessibility compared to specific-pathogen-free (SPF) counterparts (Thion et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thion et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Microglia from adult GF mice present an immature gene expression profile and fail to adequately respond to immunostimulants.
claims.source: Microglia from adult GF mice present an immature gene expression profile and fail to adequately respond to immunostimulants (Erny et al., 2015; Thion et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Erny et al., 2015 and Thion et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Feeding GF mice a mixture of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) is sufficient to rescue microglial maturation.
claims.source: However, feeding GF mice a mixture of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), metabolic products of bacterial fiber fermentation, is sufficient to rescue microglial maturation (Erny et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Erny et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Levels of SCFAs are reduced in fecal samples from PD patients compared to matched controls.
claims.source: Interestingly, levels of SCFAs are reduced in fecal samples from PD patients compared to matched controls (Chen et al., 2022; Unger et al., 2016) and inversely correlate with disease severity (Aho et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2022 and Unger et al., 2016.

claims.claim: SCFA levels inversely correlate with PD disease severity.
claims.source: Interestingly, levels of SCFAs are reduced in fecal samples from PD patients compared to matched controls (Chen et al., 2022; Unger et al., 2016) and inversely correlate with disease severity (Aho et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aho et al., 2021 and Chen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The ASO mouse model recapitulates many hallmark symptoms of PD including motor deficits, GI abnormalities, olfactory dysfunction, and neuroinflammation.
claims.source: Herein, we explore the interplay between diet and microglia in the ASO mouse model, which recapitulates many of the hallmark symptoms of PD including motor deficits, GI abnormalities, olfactory dysfunction, and neuroinflammation (Chesselet et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chesselet et al., 2012.

claims.claim: A prebiotic diet remodels the gut microbiome of ASO mice to contain increased relative abundances of taxa linked to outcomes associated with health.
claims.source: We demonstrate that a prebiotic diet remodels the gut microbiome of ASO mice to contain increased relative abundances of taxa linked to outcomes associated with health.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from metagenomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits in ASO mice.
claims.source: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits and reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice in a microglia-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior test data presented in Figure 1A-D.

claims.claim: Prebiotic intervention reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice.
claims.source: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits and reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice in a microglia-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data presented in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The beneficial effects of prebiotic intervention in ASO mice are microglia-dependent.
claims.source: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits and reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice in a microglia-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microglial depletion experiments using PLX5622 presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Prebiotic diet alters the morphology and gene expression patterns of microglia in brain regions involved in PD.
claims.source: Prebiotic diet alters the morphology and gene expression patterns of microglia in brain regions involved in PD, promoting phenotypes associated with disease-protective responses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data (Figure 3) and scRNA-seq data (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Microglial depletion abrogates the beneficial effects of prebiotics in ASO mice.
claims.source: Importantly, microglial depletion abrogates the beneficial effects of prebiotics.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from PLX5622 treatment experiments shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Enhanced metabolism of dietary fiber by the gut microbiome alters the physiology of cells in the CNS and improves behavioral and pathologic outcomes in ASO mice.
claims.source: Overall, this study reveals that enhanced metabolism of dietary fiber by the gut microbiome alters the physiology of cells in the CNS and ultimately improves behavioral and pathologic outcomes in a mouse model of PD.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim integrating multiple experimental findings from the study.

claims.claim: Three custom high-fiber diets were generated, each containing 20% of a prebiotic mixture of two or three dietary fibers.
claims.source: We generated three custom high-fiber diets (Supplementary file 1), each containing 20% of a prebiotic mixture of two or three dietary fibers designed to promote growth of distinct gut bacterial taxa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and boost SCFA production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E) based on in vitro fecal fermentation.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by data in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The prebiotic diets were designed to promote growth of distinct gut bacterial taxa and boost SCFA production based on in vitro fecal fermentation.
claims.source: We generated three custom high-fiber diets (Supplementary file 1), each containing 20% of a prebiotic mixture of two or three dietary fibers designed to promote growth of distinct gut bacterial taxa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and boost SCFA production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E) based on in vitro fecal fermentation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro fermentation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Administration of prebiotic diet #1 to ASO mice enhanced performance in pole descent and beam traversal tests compared to mice fed a control diet.
claims.source: Remarkably, administration of the prebiotic diet to ASO mice enhanced performance in several motor behavioral tests, including the pole descent and beam traversal tests (time to cross, steps to cross, errors per step) compared to mice fed a control diet (Figure 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claims.claim: Outcomes in adhesive removal, wire hang, and hindlimb score tests were unchanged by prebiotic diet.
claims.source: Outcomes in other paradigms including adhesive removal, wire hang, and hindlimb score were unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C.

claims.claim: A gut-targeting intervention has the potential to attenuate key behavioral features in a mouse model of PD.
claims.source: These findings reveal that a gut-targeting intervention has the potential to attenuate key behavioral features in a mouse model of PD.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motor behavior improvements observed with prebiotic treatment.

claims.claim: Levels of all major SCFAs were higher in fecal samples from prebiotic-fed mice than from control-fed mice.
claims.source: As anticipated, levels of all major SCFAs were higher in fecal samples from prebiotic-fed mice than from control-fed mice (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SCFA measurement data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Concentrations of propionate, butyrate, and isobutyrate were not significantly different between wild type (WT) and ASO mice fed a control diet.
claims.source: Concentrations of propionate, butyrate, and isobutyrate were not significantly different between wild type (WT) and ASO mice fed a control diet (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SCFA measurement data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: ASO mice weighed significantly less than their WT counterparts.
claims.source: ASO mice weighed significantly less than their WT counterparts and exhibited reduced food intake of control diet, but not prebiotic diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by weight and food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E.

claims.claim: ASO mice exhibited reduced food intake of control diet, but not prebiotic diet.
claims.source: ASO mice weighed significantly less than their WT counterparts and exhibited reduced food intake of control diet, but not prebiotic diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claims.claim: Prebiotic-ASO mice ate significantly more than control-ASO mice.
claims.source: While prebiotic-ASO mice ate significantly more than control-ASO mice, no difference in body weight was detected between the groups at 22 weeks of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claims.claim: No difference in body weight was detected between prebiotic-ASO and control-ASO mice at 22 weeks of age.
claims.source: While prebiotic-ASO mice ate significantly more than control-ASO mice, no difference in body weight was detected between the groups at 22 weeks of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by weight data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: Prebiotic feeding significantly reduced αSyn aggregation in the substantia nigra of ASO mice compared to control diet.
claims.source: We found a significant reduction in αSyn aggregation in the substantia nigra (SN) of prebiotic-fed ASO mice compared to ASO mice on control chow (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Prebiotic intervention had no effect on αSyn aggregation in the striatum.
claims.source: In contrast, prebiotic intervention had no effect on αSyn aggregation in the striatum (STR) (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Regional differences in microglia density, gene expression, and clearance activity may explain differential effects of prebiotics on αSyn aggregation in SN versus striatum.
claims.source: We speculate that this difference may be attributable to regional differences in microglia density, gene expression, and clearance activity (Grabert et al., 2016; Y.-L. Tan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Grabert et al., 2016 and Y.-L. Tan et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Early intervention with a prebiotic diet can reduce PD-like symptoms and brain pathology in ASO mice.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that early intervention with a prebiotic diet can reduce PD-like symptoms and brain pathology in ASO mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motor behavior and αSyn aggregation data.

claims.claim: Alpha diversity analysis revealed significant reduction in observed species count, Shannon's diversity, and Simpson's evenness in prebiotic-fed groups.
claims.source: Alpha diversity analysis revealed significant reduction in observed species count, Shannon's diversity, and Simpson's evenness in prebiotic-fed groups, as well as an increase in Gini's dominance (Figure 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic diversity analysis data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claims.claim: Prebiotic-fed groups showed an increase in Gini's dominance.
claims.source: Alpha diversity analysis revealed significant reduction in observed species count, Shannon's diversity, and Simpson's evenness in prebiotic-fed groups, as well as an increase in Gini's dominance (Figure 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic diversity analysis data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Reduced microbiome diversity in high-fiber fed mice is consistent with a previous report.
claims.source: This is consistent with a previous report of reduced microbiome diversity in high-fiber fed mice (Luo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Fecal samples clustered more closely by diet than mouse genotype in principal coordinate analysis.
claims.source: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) of species abundance showed that samples clustered more closely by diet than mouse genotype (Figure 2E) and PERMANOVA revealed that prebiotic treatment explained 6-fold more variance than genotype, with R2 values of 0.334 and 0.053 for each, respectively (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PCoA and PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2E-F.

claims.claim: Prebiotic treatment explained 6-fold more variance than genotype in microbiome composition (R2 values of 0.334 vs 0.053).
claims.source: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) of species abundance showed that samples clustered more closely by diet than mouse genotype (Figure 2E) and PERMANOVA revealed that prebiotic treatment explained 6-fold more variance than genotype, with R2 values of 0.334 and 0.053 for each, respectively (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The prebiotic diet reshapes gut microbial communities in WT and ASO mice.
claims.source: Thus, the prebiotic diet reshapes gut microbial communities in WT and ASO mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the metagenomic analysis data.

claims.claim: Prebiotic diet feeding resulted in an increase in Bacteroidetes and a decrease in Firmicutes, resulting in a lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio.
claims.source: We observed broad changes at the microbial phylum and genus levels following administration of prebiotic diet (Figure 2G and I), displaying an increase in Bacteroidetes and a decrease in Firmicutes in prebiotic diet-fed mice, resulting in a lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio that has been associated with general features of metabolic health (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claims.claim: A lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio has been associated with general features of metabolic health.
claims.source: We observed broad changes at the microbial phylum and genus levels following administration of prebiotic diet (Figure 2G and I), displaying an increase in Bacteroidetes and a decrease in Firmicutes in prebiotic diet-fed mice, resulting in a lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio that has been associated with general features of metabolic health (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the F/B ratio and metabolic health.

claims.claim: Bacteroidetes are reduced in PD patients compared to age-matched controls.
claims.source: Intriguingly, it has been shown that Bacteroidetes are reduced in PD patients compared to age-matched controls, suggesting the prebiotic may counter this effect (Unger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Unger et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Prebiotic diet resulted in a decrease in Proteobacteria, a phylum often increased in dysbiosis and inflammation and elevated in PD patient fecal samples.
claims.source: Additionally, we observed a decrease in Proteobacteria, a phylum often increased in dysbiosis and inflammation and elevated in PD patient fecal samples (Figure 2H; Keshavarzian et al., 2015; Shin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic data in Figure 2H and citations to Keshavarzian et al., 2015 and Shin et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Gut-brain module analysis showed variation in metabolic pathways including SCFA degradation/synthesis in response to diet and genotype.
claims.source: Gut-brain module analysis showed variation in metabolic pathways including SCFA degradation/synthesis in response to diet and genotype (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gut-brain module analysis data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: Feeding of a prebiotic diet restructures the ASO microbiome toward increased relative abundances of taxa associated with potentially protective effects.
claims.source: Overall, feeding of a prebiotic diet appears to qualitatively restructure the ASO microbiome toward increased relative abundances of taxa associated with potentially protective effects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the metagenomic analysis data.

claims.claim: In ASO mice, microglia reactivity in response to αSyn overexpression appears at 4–5 weeks of age in the STR and at 20–24 weeks of age in the SN.
claims.source: In ASO mice, microglia reactivity in response to αSyn overexpression appears at 4–5 weeks of age in the STR and at 20–24 weeks of age in the SN (Watson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2012.

claims.claim: SCFAs have been shown to influence the physiology of microglia in several contexts.
claims.source: SCFAs have been shown to influence the physiology of microglia in several contexts (Colombo et al., 2021; Erny et al., 2015; Sadler et al., 2020; Erny et al., 2021; Sampson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Homeostatic microglia exhibit a ramified shape with a smaller cell body and increased dendritic processes.
claims.source: The morphology of microglia can indicate their reactivity state, with homeostatic microglia exhibiting a ramified shape with a smaller cell body and increased dendritic processes, whereas activated microglia adopt an amoeboid form with a larger cell body and retracted processes (Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018.

claims.claim: Activated microglia adopt an amoeboid form with a larger cell body and retracted processes.
claims.source: The morphology of microglia can indicate their reactivity state, with homeostatic microglia exhibiting a ramified shape with a smaller cell body and increased dendritic processes, whereas activated microglia adopt an amoeboid form with a larger cell body and retracted processes (Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018.

claims.claim: Microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice had significantly smaller cell bodies than in control-ASO mice.
claims.source: We observed that microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice had significantly smaller cell bodies than in control-ASO mice (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by IBA1 immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: Microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice exhibited increased dendrite length, number of segments, number of branch points, and number of terminal points compared to control-ASO mice.
claims.source: 3D analysis of key morphological features revealed that microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice exhibited increased dendrite length, number of segments, number of branch points, and number of terminal points compared to microglia from control-ASO mice (Figure 3C–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction analysis data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claims.claim: Long-term prebiotic intervention dampens microglial reactivity in brain regions implicated in PD.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings indicate that long-term prebiotic intervention dampens microglial reactivity in brain regions implicated in PD.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the microglial morphology data.

claims.claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 313 differentially expressed genes (163 upregulated, 150 downregulated) in the SN between control-WT and control-ASO mice.
claims.source: Differential gene expression analysis of all cells revealed 313 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (↑163, ↓150, FDR <0.05) in the SN and 997 DEGs (↑511, ↓486) in the STR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 997 differentially expressed genes (511 upregulated, 486 downregulated) in the STR between control-WT and control-ASO mice.
claims.source: Differential gene expression analysis of all cells revealed 313 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (↑163, ↓150, FDR <0.05) in the SN and 997 DEGs (↑511, ↓486) in the STR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: In the SN, microglia from control-ASO mice displayed increased expression of MHC class I components, several chemokines and chemokine receptors, and pro-inflammatory markers.
claims.source: In the SN, microglia harvested from control-ASO mice displayed increased expression of MHC class I components (H2-K1, H2-D1), several chemokines (Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl9) and chemokine receptors (Ccr1, Ccr5), and pro-inflammatory markers (Nfkbid, Cd 74) (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2a.

claims.claim: Gene enrichment analysis of upregulated DEGs in control-ASO mice showed enrichment in pathways related to cellular responses to cytokine stimulus and interferon-gamma, immune system processes, and response to stress.
claims.source: Gene enrichment analysis of all upregulated DEGs in control-ASO mice showed enrichment in pathways related to cellular responses to cytokine stimulus and interferon-gamma, immune system processes, and response to stress (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Several genes downregulated in control-ASO mice compared to control-WT were related to anti-inflammatory signaling and microglial homeostasis.
claims.source: Several genes that were downregulated in control-ASO mice compared to control-WT were related to anti-inflammatory signaling (Klf2, Klf4) and microglial homeostasis (P2ry12, Slc2a5) (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2a.

claims.claim: Control-ASO microglia in the STR upregulated pro-inflammatory modulators and antigen processing and presentation genes.
claims.source: We observed similar trends in the STR, with control-ASO microglia upregulating pro-inflammatory modulators (Tnf, Nfkbiz, Trim8, Irgm1) and antigen processing and presentation genes (H2-Q7, H2-K1, H2-D1, H2-T23) and downregulating genes related to homeostatic cellular processes (Figure 4H–I, Supplementary file 2c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4H-I and Supplementary file 2c.

claims.claim: The anti-inflammatory cytokine transforming growth factor beta 2 (Tgfβ2) was ~45-fold downregulated in control-ASO microglia in the STR.
claims.source: Notably, the anti-inflammatory cytokine transforming growth factor beta 2 (Tgfβ2) was ~45-fold downregulated in control-ASO (Supplementary file 2c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data in Supplementary file 2c.

claims.claim: Microglia from control-ASO mice upregulate pro-inflammatory immune processes and downregulate pathways related to homeostasis and cellular maintenance in response to αSyn overexpression.
claims.source: These data suggest microglia from control-ASO mice upregulate pro-inflammatory immune processes and downregulate pathways related to homeostasis and cellular maintenance in response to αSyn overexpression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the scRNA-seq differential expression data.

claims.claim: UMAP analysis yielded nine distinct microglia clusters in the SN and eight clusters in the STR based on global scRNA-seq gene expression.
claims.source: Based on global scRNA-seq gene expression, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction (UMAP) analysis yielded nine distinct microglia clusters in the SN and eight clusters in the STR (Figure 4A and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by UMAP analysis shown in Figure 4A and F.

claims.claim: The percentage of microglia in cluster 0 was higher in control-ASO than control-WT mice (27.1% vs 18.9%), and prebiotic treatment reduced this to 18.3%.
claims.source: Interestingly, the percentage of microglia in cluster 0 was higher in control-ASO than control-WT mice (27.1% vs 18.9%), and prebiotic treatment reduced the percentage of microglia belonging to cluster 0 in ASO mice compared to control diets (18.3%) (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Gene enrichment analysis of cluster 0 revealed pathways related to immune system processes, cellular response to TNF, cellular response to lipopolysaccharide, and response to stress.
claims.source: Gene enrichment analysis of the top 50 genes associated with cluster 0 revealed pathways related to immune system processes, cellular response to tumor necrosis factor (TNF), cellular response to lipopolysaccharide, and response to stress.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis of cluster 0.

claims.claim: Cluster 0 contained several prominent immune markers including Tnf, Nfkbia, Ccl2, Ccl3, and Ccl4.
claims.source: Cluster 0 contained several prominent immune markers including Tnf, Nfkbia, Ccl2, Ccl3, and Ccl4, suggesting that a prebiotic diet may suppress or prevent pro-inflammatory responses in ASO mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq cluster analysis data.

claims.claim: Levels of TNF and Ccl2 are elevated in the serum of PD patients.
claims.source: Notably, levels of TNF and Ccl2 are elevated in the serum of PD patients (Brodacki et al., 2008; Reale et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brodacki et al., 2008 and Reale et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The percentage of microglia belonging to cluster 2 was reduced in control-ASO mice but increased in prebiotic-ASO mice.
claims.source: Conversely, the percentage of microglia belonging to cluster 2 was reduced in control-ASO mice but increased in prebiotic-ASO mice (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Among the most highly expressed genes in cluster 2 were the homeostatic microglial markers P2ry12 and Cst3, as well as the anti-inflammatory transcription factors Klf2 and Klf4.
claims.source: Among the most highly expressed genes in cluster 2 were the homeostatic microglial markers P2ry12 and Cst3, as well as the anti-inflammatory transcription factors Klf2 and Klf4 (Das et al., 2006; Li et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq cluster analysis data and citations to Das et al., 2006 and Li et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The top 10 associative genes in cluster 3 in the STR included several mitochondrial genes.
claims.source: The top 10 associative genes in cluster 3 included several mitochondrial genes: mt-Atp6, mt-Cytb, mt-Co2, mt-Co3, mt-Nd4, mt-Nd1, and mt-Nd2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq cluster analysis data.

claims.claim: A 13.4% increase in cluster 1 was detected in control-ASO mice, with prebiotic diet restoring the percentage back to control-WT levels.
claims.source: Additionally, we detected a 13.4% increase in cluster 1 in control-ASO mice, with prebiotic diet restoring the percentage of cluster 1 back to control-WT levels (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Significantly enriched pathways within cluster 1 included those positively regulating cell death and immune system development, and negatively regulating cellular processes.
claims.source: The significantly enriched pathways within cluster 1 included those positively regulating cell death and immune system development, and negatively regulating cellular processes, suggesting increased immune signaling and dysregulation of homeostatic signaling in the absence of prebiotic treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis of cluster 1.

claims.claim: Comparison of prebiotic-ASO to control-ASO microglia found 473 DEGs (317 upregulated, 156 downregulated) in the SN and 1474 DEGs (608 upregulated, 866 downregulated) in the STR.
claims.source: To determine effects of long-term prebiotic exposure on microglial gene expression in ASO mice, we compared prebiotic-ASO microglia to control-ASO and found 473 DEGs (↑317, ↓156) in the SN and 1474 DEGs (↑608, ↓866) in the STR (Figure 4C and H, Supplementary file 2b, d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: Gene enrichment analysis of the 156 genes downregulated in prebiotic-ASO microglia in the SN revealed reduction in IL-1β production pathways, innate immune response, and defense response pathways.
claims.source: Gene enrichment analysis of the 156 genes downregulated in prebiotic-ASO microglia in the SN revealed reduction in interleukin-1 (IL-1)β production pathways, as well as dampened innate immune response and defense response pathways compared to control-ASO mice (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Among the genes downregulated in microglia from prebiotic-ASO mice were several mediators of pro-inflammatory immune response, antigen presentation and processing, and chemokines/receptors.

results.result: A prebiotic diet containing 20% dietary fiber improved motor performance in ASO mice on pole descent and beam traversal tests, increased fecal SCFA levels, but did not affect other motor tests. ASO mice showed reduced body weight and food intake on control diet, which was normalized on prebiotic diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C40 provide convergent evidence from multiple motor tests (C32-C33), SCFA measurements (C35-C36), and metabolic parameters (C37-C40). The selective improvement in specific motor tests is appropriately documented with negative results reported for other paradigms. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=16-29) with appropriate statistical testing.

results.result: Prebiotic diet significantly reduced α-synuclein aggregation in the substantia nigra but not the striatum of ASO mice, suggesting region-specific effects potentially related to differences in microglial density and clearance activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 demonstrate clear regional specificity in α-synuclein pathology reduction supported by dot blot quantification. The speculation about mechanisms (C43) is appropriately qualified and supported by citations. This represents a key pathological outcome measure directly relevant to PD.

results.result: Prebiotic diet substantially remodeled the gut microbiome composition in ASO mice, reducing alpha diversity while increasing Bacteroidetes and decreasing Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, resulting in a microbiome profile associated with metabolic health.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C56 present comprehensive metagenomic analysis with appropriate diversity metrics, PCoA, and PERMANOVA statistics. The finding that diet explained 6-fold more variance than genotype (R²=0.334 vs 0.053) is statistically robust. The interpretation linking these changes to health is supported by citations and established knowledge, though causality to behavioral outcomes requires the mechanistic studies that follow.

results.result: Prebiotic diet altered microglial morphology in ASO mice, reducing cell body size and increasing dendritic complexity (length, segments, branch points, terminal points) in both substantia nigra and striatum, indicating reduced microglial reactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 provide quantitative morphological data from immunofluorescence and 3D reconstruction analysis. The interpretation (C63) appropriately integrates established knowledge about microglial morphology-function relationships (C59-C60). Sample sizes (n=5/group for diameter, 3-5 cells/mouse for 3D reconstruction) are modest but adequate for this type of analysis.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq revealed that control-ASO mice exhibit increased pro-inflammatory gene expression (MHC class I, chemokines, pro-inflammatory markers) and decreased homeostatic/anti-inflammatory genes in microglia from both substantia nigra and striatum compared to control-WT mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C71 present comprehensive scRNA-seq differential expression analysis with appropriate FDR correction (FDR<0.05) and gene enrichment analysis. The identification of 313 DEGs in SN and 997 in STR with consistent pro-inflammatory signatures provides strong molecular characterization of the ASO model. The notable 45-fold downregulation of Tgfβ2 (C70) is particularly striking.

results.result: UMAP clustering analysis identified distinct microglial subpopulations in ASO mice, with prebiotic treatment reducing the percentage of pro-inflammatory cluster 0 (containing TNF, Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4) and increasing homeostatic cluster 2 (containing P2ry12, Cst3, Klf2, Klf4) in the substantia nigra.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C81 demonstrate sophisticated single-cell analysis revealing functionally distinct microglial states. The shift from 27.1% to 18.3% in cluster 0 with prebiotic treatment (C73) and the reciprocal changes in cluster 2 (C77) provide clear evidence of phenotypic modulation. The connection to PD patient biomarkers (C76) strengthens translational relevance.

results.result: Prebiotic intervention in ASO mice downregulated pro-inflammatory pathways (IL-1β production, innate immunity, defense response) and upregulated disease-associated macrophage (DAM) markers including Trem2 in microglia, suggesting induction of a neuroprotective phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C90 provide strong evidence for prebiotic-induced transcriptional reprogramming with 473 DEGs in SN and 1474 in STR. The identification of DAM markers (C87, C89) and their association with neuroprotection (C88) is well-supported by citations. However, the functional significance of DAM induction in this context would benefit from additional validation beyond transcriptional signatures.

results.result: SCFAs do not accumulate in brain tissue of prebiotic-fed mice, and microglia show minimal expression of SCFA receptors (FFAR2/3) and no changes in chromatin accessibility or HDAC expression, suggesting indirect mechanisms of microglial modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 present negative results that are critical for mechanistic understanding. The absence of brain SCFA accumulation (C91), minimal FFAR expression (C93), unchanged ATAC-seq profiles (C94), and stable HDAC expression (C95) collectively argue against direct SCFA signaling in the brain. The conclusion of indirect mechanisms (C96) is appropriately cautious and acknowledges limitations.

results.result: Microglial depletion using PLX5622 eliminated the beneficial effects of prebiotic diet on motor performance and α-synuclein aggregation in ASO mice, demonstrating that microglia are required for prebiotic-mediated neuroprotection.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C106 provide compelling loss-of-function evidence for microglial necessity. The regional variation in depletion efficiency (C98) is appropriately documented, and the finding that even partial depletion (~65-75%) abolished prebiotic benefits (C101) strengthens the conclusion. The observation that depletion had no effect in control-fed mice (C104) but increased α-synuclein in prebiotic-fed mice (C105) is particularly informative about microglial function.

results.result: PLX5622 treatment showed relatively high specificity for brain microglia, with minimal effects on gut-associated immune populations except for modest reductions in CSF1Rlo lymphocytes in large intestine and spleen.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 provide important specificity controls for the PLX5622 depletion experiments through comprehensive flow cytometry analysis of peripheral immune populations. The finding of brain-specific effects (C111) strengthens the interpretation that behavioral and pathological changes are microglia-dependent rather than due to peripheral immune alterations.

results.result: The mechanism by which prebiotic diet influences microglial physiology remains unclear, but likely involves indirect effects through peripheral immunity rather than direct SCFA signaling in the brain, with other microbial metabolites potentially contributing.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 appropriately acknowledge mechanistic uncertainty while synthesizing negative findings about direct SCFA effects. The speculation about peripheral immune modulation (C116) is reasonable given the evidence, though it remains untested. The acknowledgment of alternative metabolites (C117) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The effects of SCFAs on microglia and behavior are highly context-dependent, with oral SCFA administration inducing microglial reactivity in germ-free mice but sodium butyrate reducing reactivity in MPTP mice with intact microbiota, highlighting the importance of experimental context.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 synthesize findings from multiple studies to contextualize the current results. The citations appropriately support the contrasting effects of SCFAs in different experimental contexts. The conclusion about considering context (C121) is well-justified and important for interpreting diet-microbiome studies.

results.result: Microglial depletion has context-dependent effects across neurodegenerative disease models, with no effect on motor performance in control-diet ASO mice but elimination of prebiotic benefits, suggesting microglia are specifically required for diet-mediated neuroprotection.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C126 appropriately contextualize the PLX5622 findings within the broader literature on microglial depletion.
